extracted.intended_audience: poets and creative writers (especially American poets and proponents of a democratic, naturalistic poetic practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing poetry appropriate to a democratic New World: poems should be candid, natural, scientifically informed, socially inclusive, engaged with the present age, and aimed at enduring, universal effect. Emphasizes style, subject-matter, ethics of authorship, and social function of the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be the channel, not the ornamenter
rubrics_metrics.description: The great poet is 'more the channel of thoughts and things without increase or diminution' and vows 'I will not be meddlesome... I will have nothing hang in the way, not the richest curtains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting affected elegance, tricks, or decorative effects between your subject and the reader; let what you tell stand precisely as it is so the reader 'stand by my side and look in the mirror with me.' Anti-pattern: putting stylistic 'curtains' or artifice that distracts from the thing described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconstraint and original practical example
rubrics_metrics.description: Great writers exhibit 'unconstraint' and 'silent defiance advancing from new free forms' and are 'greatest... who contributes the greatest original practical example.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize freedom from precedent and show originality by providing concrete, practical examples or new forms rather than mere theory. Innovation should be practical and demonstrative rather than ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create or find the proper sphere for expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'cleanest expression is that which finds no sphere worthy of itself, and makes one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If existing forms or genres do not fit what you must say, fashion a form or space that does. Expression may legitimately invent its own context rather than force content into an ill-fitting tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address readers on equal terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The messages of great poems are 'Come to us on equal terms'—poems must approach readers as equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write inclusively and democratically; avoid elitist tone. The poem's invitation should be one of parity so readers can truly 'understand us.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace multiple kinds of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirms 'there can be unnumber'd Supremes, and that one does not countervail another'—many modes of greatness coexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prescribing a single canonical style or standard of genius; recognize and cultivate varied voices and forms of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity and encouragement toward competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: American bards 'shall be mark'd for generosity and affection, and for encouraging competitors... glad to pass anything to any one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share knowledge, models, and resources; do not hoard recognition or seek monopoly. Social practice of generosity is part of the poet's virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow class- or region-based depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The American bard 'shall delineate no class of persons, nor one or two out of the strata of interests... and not be for the Eastern States more than the Western, or the Northern States more than the Southern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for breadth in subject and sympathy; do not write only for or about a privileged stratum or region. Anti-pattern: limiting poetry's concern to narrow social circles or local elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exact science and practical knowledge as support
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact science and its movements are 'no checks on the greatest poet, but always his encouragement and support... the anatomist, chemist, astronomer, geologist... are not poets, but they are the lawgivers of poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on factual, empirical knowledge (scientific, technical, travel experience) to enrich imagery and underpin poetic conception; consult varied disciplines for the 'seed of the conception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground poetry in natural laws and avoid supernatural miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole theory of the supernatural 'departs as a dream' and 'The great master has nothing to do with miracles... To be under the general law is great.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations and aesthetics consistent with observable nature and human experience; avoid relying on inexplicable miracles as poetic crutches. Emphasize sanity and ensemble in depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate candidly past, present, future
rubrics_metrics.description: Men and women 'are to be taken as they are, and the investigation of their past and present and future shall be unintermitted, and shall be done with perfect candor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice honest, thorough inquiry into subjects and characters. Candor and truthful representation are normative; deceit or romantic falsification is censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament only when natural and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ornaments to a work nothing outre can be allow'd--but those ornaments can be allow'd that conform to the perfect facts of the open air... and are necessary to the completion of the work. Most works are most beautiful without ornament.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simplicity; add ornament only when it inevitably flows from the nature of the work. Anti-pattern: gratuitous or grotesque ornamentation that distorts honest shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distortion of honest shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that 'distorts honest shapes, or which creates unearthly beings or places or contingencies, is a nuisance and revolt... Of the human form especially, it is so great it must never be made ridiculous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect natural form and proportion in figurative depiction; avoid caricature, grotesque exaggeration, or bizarre inventions that repulse rather than illuminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate perfect personal candor and avoid tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poets are 'to be known by the absence in them of tricks, and by the justification of perfect personal candor. All faults may be forgiven of him who has perfect candor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be radically honest in voice and intention; transparency of the poet's perspective covers many technical faults. Anti-pattern: calculated artifice or slyness that conceals truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic character includes prudence and humane affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes such as 'extreme caution or prudence, the soundest organic health, large hope and comparison and fondness for women and children' are parts of the greatest poet from birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a balanced life and humane affections—physical health, moral prudence, and compassionate relationships—which inform and sustain poetic authority. Anti-pattern: sacrificing life and health for mere accumulation of wealth or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist reducing prudence to mere material thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence is not 'the melancholy prudence of the abandonment of such a great being as a man... to the toss and pallor of years of money-making' and 'thrift without the loving nod of the soul is only a foetid puff.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value experiential, soulful living over narrowly economic calculations; a poet's prudence should preserve conditions for full life and creativity rather than prioritize wealth accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage fully with the immediate age
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct trial is 'to-day. If he does not flood himself with the immediate age as with vast oceanic tides... let him merge in the general run.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be immersed in and responsive to contemporary life, events, and sensibilities. Poetic relevance requires absorption of the present rather than aloofness or retreat into exclusively past forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for timelessness—test by centuries
rubrics_metrics.description: The prescient poet 'projects himself centuries ahead, and judges performer or performance after the changes of time. Does it live through them? Does it still hold on untired?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with an eye toward longevity and universal human concerns; prefer qualities that will resonate across ages rather than transient fashions. Use the test: will the young, middle-aged, and old think of it long after?

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek universality across persons and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poem is 'for ages and ages in common, and for all degrees and complexions, and all departments and sects, and for a woman as much as a man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write to be intelligible and moving to diverse audiences—different sexes, classes, sects, and ages. Avoid exclusivity or appeals limited to narrow constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be a beginning that provokes action
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poem 'is no finish to a man or woman, but rather a beginning... Whom he takes he takes with firm sure grasp into live regions previously unattain'd... and shall never be quiet again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose work that incites continued thought, action, or transformation in readers; avoid producing merely decorative or conclusory pieces that leave the reader unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as priest of man—religion through democracy and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be 'no more priests... A new order shall arise, and they shall be the priests of man... They shall find their inspiration in real objects to-day... It must be consign'd henceforth to democracy en masse, and to literature. It must enter into the poems of the nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse poetry with a moral/spiritual energy grounded in democratic humanism and real life rather than ecclesiastical dogma; poems should serve as communal spiritual nourishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use language adequate to national character—plain, brawny, and flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: The English language 'befriends the grand American expression--it is brawny enough, and limber and full enough... It is the powerful language of resistance... It is the medium that shall wellnigh express the inexpressible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the strengths of the vernacular—forceful, flexible, plain speech suited to express growth, freedom, equality, and the modern age. Avoid unnecessary archaisms or foreign mannerisms that obstruct clarity and democratic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and institutions must conform to American standards of equality and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: No literature, style of behavior, public institution, or ornament 'can long elude the jealous and passionate instinct of American standards... Is it uniform with my country?... Is it for the nursing of the young of the republic?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by their fit with democratic, practical, and communal needs: do they serve the nation's growth, nourish the young, and avoid ignominious distinctions? Anti-pattern: art that is elitist, ornamental without usefulness, or alien to national life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce an imaginative New World literature aligned with modern science and politics
rubrics_metrics.description: A modern image-making creation is 'indispensable to fuse and express the modern political and scientific creations' so that 'the trinity [political, scientific, literary] will be complete.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop literature that corresponds to contemporary scientific and political realities—create new images and forms that synthesize modern life rather than mimic outdated European models. The poet's work should help build the nation's cultural edifice.
